DOCUMENT:
# 2027 Customer Support Hiring Plan

**To:** Chief Operating Officer | **From:** Support Operations | **Date:** 13 November 2026

**Decision requested:** Approve 12 net new agents in two phases: 8 starting January 11 and 4 starting in September. Separately, approve a capped vendor overflow budget for tax season.

## Recommendation

| Item | Timing | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 8 net new agents | Jan 11 class | At least 6 bilingual English/Spanish |
| 4 net new agents | Sept class | Confirmed at a July review of Q2 self-service results |
| Backfills | Monthly, 1–3 per class | Sized to actual attrition; bilingual preferred |
| Vendor overflow | Feb–Apr | Non-complaint tickets, capped at ~$150k |

The 12 net hires would cost about **$610k in 2027**, compared with $816k for 12 full-year positions.

## Demand

- **Average month in 2027:** 31,000 × 1.35 (user growth) × 0.88 (help-centre effect) ≈ **36,800 tickets**. At 740 tickets per agent, that needs about 50 fully productive agents.
- **Complaint rule:** Adding 6 minutes to about 3,300 complaint tickets a month uses about 330 agent-hours, or roughly 2.4 agents (assuming 140 productive hours per agent-month).
- **Steady-state need:** about 52 agents. Our 42 plus 12 gives 54, which covers it.

The average hides the shape of the year:

- **Tax season (Feb–Apr)** runs at about 51,600 tickets a month and needs about 70 agents. No hiring plan closes this gap. Even the January 11 class only reaches full productivity on March 22.
- **The other nine months** run about 13% below average. They need about 45 agents early in the year, rising toward 52 by Q4 as users grow.

Hiring all 12 in Q1 would leave us 6–8 agents overstaffed through mid-year and still short during tax season.

## Why this phasing

- **January (8):** Our current capacity (42 × 740 = 31,080 tickets) equals 2026 average demand, so we have no slack today. These hires will be productive before the April 1 complaint rule takes effect.
- **September (4):** These agents will be fully productive by mid-November, ahead of Q4 growth and the 2028 tax season. Waiting also shows us whether dispute tracking and card replacement reduce volume. If they do, we may need fewer.
- **Vendor for the peak:** Even after the January class, we will be short about 16,000–17,500 tickets a month. At $4.10 per ticket, the vendor is cheaper than an in-house agent (about $7.66 per ticket) for a three-month spike. Complaints must stay in-house. Capping the vendor at about 36,000 tickets means we absorb the rest as longer waits, as we did in 2026, when peak capacity was about 28% below demand.

## Spanish coverage

Spanish is 18% of volume, about 6,600 tickets a month in 2027. That needs about 9 bilingual agents, and we have 4, which explains why Spanish waits are 3.4 times longer. Weighting the January class toward bilingual hires brings us to about 10 bilingual agents by Q2. Offers must go out by mid-December, so recruiting should start bilingual sourcing now.

## Attrition is the larger risk

At 38% attrition, we lose about 18 agents a year. That is more than the net growth requested here, and each replacement loses about 5 weeks of productivity while ramping up. Exit interviews cite night-shift scheduling and below-market pay. I will bring a proposal in Q1 covering a night-shift differential or rotation and a pay benchmark. Cutting attrition to 28% would avoid about 5 replacement hires a year.

## Assumptions to confirm

- Backfills are funded within the existing 42 positions, not from the 12.
- 35% user growth means the 2027 average compared with the 2026 average.
- The 12% help-centre reduction will persist.
- Agents have about 140 productive hours per month.

---

##

FACTS:
Paybridge's support team has 42 agents. In 2026 they handled an average of 31,000 tickets per month. A fully trained agent handles about 740 tickets per month. New agents take 10 weeks to reach full productivity and average about 50% productivity during that period. The growth team projects that active users will grow 35% in 2027. In September 2026 Paybridge launched a new self-service help centre. In its first two months, tickets per active user fell 12% compared with the same months the year before. Annual agent attrition is 38%. Exit interviews mention night-shift scheduling and pay below that of local competitors. About 18% of tickets are in Spanish. The team has 4 bilingual agents, and English-only agents cannot handle Spanish tickets. Average wait time for Spanish tickets is 3.4 times longer than for English tickets. A new rule from the state financial regulator takes effect April 1, 2027. It requires every customer complaint to receive a written response within 15 days and to be recorded in a complaint log. Support leads estimate that this will add about 6 minutes of handling time to each complaint ticket. Complaints are currently about 9% of tickets. Ticket volume is seasonal. From February through April, during tax season, volume runs about 40% above the annual monthly average. The COO has approved a budget for 12 net new agent positions in 2027. Loaded cost is $68,000 per agent per year. The recruiting team can run one training class a month of up to 8 new hires. The next available class start date is January 11. The VP of Product has said that two more self-service features (dispute status tracking and card replacement) will launch in Q2 and could reduce tickets further, but no estimate of the effect has been provided. Finance has suggested outsourcing overflow tickets to a vendor at $4.10 per ticket. Compliance has said that complaint tickets may not be outsourced.

KNOWN COMPLICATIONS:
- Ticket volume will not grow at the same rate as users: a 35% rise in users combined with a 12% drop in tickets per user means about 19% more tickets (1.35 x 0.88 = 1.188), about 36,800 a month, not 41,850.
- Spanish tickets are a separate bottleneck. Spanish volume (about 5,580 a month now) needs about 7.5 agents, but there are only 4 bilingual agents. A total headcount figure hides this gap.
- With 38% attrition, about 16 agents a year will leave and need replacing, in addition to net growth. Training takes 10 weeks, and the February-April peak means agents need to start in December or January to help at all.
- The new regulator rule adds handling time from April and complaint tickets cannot be outsourced, which affects how much the outsourcing option can help, and the result may still exceed the budget of 12 net hires.

AUTHOR'S ANTICIPATED CRITIQUES:
1. **The help-centre effect rests on thin evidence.** Two months of data may reflect novelty. Part of the effect may also already be in the 2026 average, since the help centre launched in September. Applying the full 12% risks understating demand.
2. **The 140-hour figure is assumed, not sourced.** The complaint workload estimate depends directly on it.
3. **The vendor spend sits outside the headcount budget.** The plan uses unspent hiring money to justify a separate spending request, which may not be fungible.
4. **The vendor cost comparison is too favourable.** It ignores repeat contacts, quality and escalations, vendor management, data-security review for a payments app, vendor ramp time, and contract minimums. It also doesn't confirm the vendor can handle Spanish.
5. **The plan sizes for throughput, not service levels.** No wait-time target is stated, and running near 100% utilisation produces long queues. The "overstaffed" claim may be wrong.
6. **The peak estimate ignores growth timing.** Feb–Apr sits early on the growth curve, which likely overstates the peak and understates Q4.
7. **Attrition among new hires isn't modelled.** Early-tenure attrition is usually above average, so the January class may shrink.
8. **The class cap isn't reconciled.** January backfills plus 8 net hires exceed the 8-person limit. Trainer, QA, and team-lead capacity are not addressed.
9. **Bilingual hiring in 8 weeks is optimistic.** It likely requires a language premium, which interacts with the existing pay complaints.
10. **The 15-day response requirement is treated only as handling time.** Complaint backlogs during the April peak are a compliance risk, since complaints can't be outsourced.
11. **The September gate has no criteria.** The plan doesn't say what Q2 result would cancel or expand the September class.
12. **Night-shift coverage isn't addressed.** The plan doesn't specify which shifts new hires fill, even though night shifts drive attrition.
13. **Alternatives aren't compared.** For example, it doesn't cost out all 12 hires in Q1 or estimate the customer churn caused by long waits.

FINDINGS:
- The January class is entirely net new hires, so the table's claim of monthly backfills is false for January and December/January attrition goes unreplaced into tax season.
- Attrition drag (about 18 departures a year, each costing ramp-up productivity and vacancy time) is left out of the capacity math, which erodes roughly 2 FTE and weakens the claim that 54 agents covers demand.
- The memo never states that combined headcount and vendor cost (about $760k) falls within the $816k already approved, and it leaves unclear whether the vendor needs new money.
- The timeline omits that the vendor must be contracted and onboarded now to be live by February.
- The memo does not say whether the vendor can handle Spanish tickets, which determines whether vendor overflow helps or worsens the Spanish gap.
- The July review may come too early to evaluate the Q2 features if they launch in late June, leaving the September decision on thin evidence.
- Spanish coverage at peak is not addressed: nine bilingual agents cover only the average month while peak demand needs about 12–13, and bilingual attrition calls for bilingual backfills.
- The cost comparison ($4.10 vendor vs. $7.66 in-house per ticket) invites the question of why not outsource year-round, and the memo does not explain why in-house is preferred off-peak.
- The mid-December offer deadline is not sourced from the brief and is not labeled as either recruiting's input or the author's estimate.
- The statement 'No hiring plan closes this gap' is overstated, because 28 hires would close it; it should be limited to the 12 approved positions.
- Labeling the annual average of about 52 as 'Steady-state need' appears to contradict the stated off-peak need of 45–52.
- The assumptions list omits key assumptions: complaints staying at about 9% of tickets, seasonality matching 2026, and the vendor being live by February.
- The draft appears to exceed the brief's 600-word limit.
